KEY MESSAGE 1...Coastal low pressure to bring light to moderate rain
Sunday.

The current setup at the surface features continued high
pressure across the area although the center of this ridge has
moved north of the Mason-Dixon Line. To the south, an inverted
trough extends along the southeastern U.S. coastline while a
wavy frontal zone stretches across central Florida to the north
of the Bahamas. Over the next 24 to 36 hours, the persistent
ridge pulls up into New England and eventually the Canadian
Maritimes. At the same time, the frontal system around Florida
is slated to lift northward, generally paralleling the Atlantic
coastline. How close the accompanying waves of embedded low
pressure will dictate the level of local impacts to the region.

For the weekend, the more tranquil day of weather would be
today/Saturday owing to residual high pressure. However, unlike
previous days this week, clouds will be on the increase as
moisture lifts poleward from the southeastern U.S. The GOES-19 
multi-layer water vapor channels show ample mid/high level
moisture streaming north away from multiple convective
complexes. After a chilly start to the morning, particularly in
more rural/low-lying areas, expect nocturnal radiation
inversions to mix out with daytime heating. Filtered sunshine
through the cirrus canopy will help usher high temperatures into
the low/mid 60s, with 50s across mountain locales. Winds
gradually shift to easterly onshore as the inverted coastal
trough approaches. Any rain chances look to hold off until late
tonight, perhaps longer given dry low-level profiles to start.

Despite rain only being 24 hours away from arriving, there
remains discernible forecast spread. While some solutions are
notably dry (i.e., 00Z GFS, AI GFS, previous 12Z NSSL MPAS),
there are still models producing 1 to 2 inches over the region
(i.e., 00Z Canadian Regional (RDPS) and multiple 06Z REFS
members). For now, will continue to play the situation
conservatively with a broad 0.10 to 0.25 inches over the area, 
accompanied by pockets approaching 0.50 inches toward the 
Chesapeake Bay. With a more offshore track of the series of 
lows, the strength of north to northeasterly winds decreased as 
well. However, any westward shift would bring back some of the 
stronger winds currently slated to be across the western 
Atlantic Ocean. Outside of the rain chances, high temperatures 
will mainly be in the mid 50s to mid 60s. The forecast looks dry
for the start of the new work week as an upstream cold front 
moves through early Monday. A downsloping northwesterly wind 
will still help raise temperatures well into the 60s. This also 
produces a favorable upslope flow to produce some light showers 
along/west of the Allegheny Front. These wind down by Monday 
afternoon with a seasonably cool night looming ahead.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Cooler conditions are expected next week, with a
coastal low forecast to track up the East Coast around
Thanksgiving.

A stronger surge of cold advection will arrive Monday night behind a 
secondary cold front. Temperatures will subsequently turn slightly 
below normal Tuesday into Wednesday as high pressure builds across 
the Great Lakes and toward New England.

An elongated trough axis will quickly progress from the Rockies 
toward the Appalachians during mid week. There will likely be two 
embedded shortwaves, one emanating from the Desert Southwest 
and the other from the Canadian Rockies but lagging longitudinally.
How these two feature eventually interact (if at all), and 
subsequent cyclogenesis along the East Coast will play an 
important role in local impacts for the Thanksgiving timeframe. 
This far out, both deterministic and ensemble guidance show a 
wide range of potential solutions, so it's far too early to get 
into specific details. However, at least some precipitation 
appears likely, especially closer to the coast. Current ensemble
guidance suggests that precipitation would most likely fall as 
rain at lower elevations, with greater chances for wintry 
precipitation at higher elevations, especially across western 
portions of the forecast area. Recent guidance has been trending
higher precipitation amounts away from the Alleghenies, but the
forecast remains dynamic and worth monitoring.

Unless a deeper closed low develops, any precipitation likely exits 
by Friday. The progressive upper level pattern keeps the coldest air 
bottled up well to the north, so expect continued seasonable 
temperatures for the end of the week.
